digest.top_line: AGITG MASTERPLAN: adding SBRT 40 Gy/5 fx to chemo cut 12-mo LRR 20.2% vs 52.0% (P=0.022) in high-risk/BR/LA pancreas; mOS 22.0 vs 14.0 mo.
digest.tldr: Pancreas and breast carry the RT news: MASTERPLAN adds SBRT to chemo with LRR and mOS gains, while TOP-1 omitting both RT and ET in women ≥70 with low-risk ER+ BC gave 5-yr LR 14.8%, above its 10% threshold. UNION's SCRT → camrelizumab + CAPOX lifts LARC 3-yr EFS, but RT and PD-1 effects are confounded.

sites.intro: Randomized de-escalation of adjuvant radioiodine in DTC via I-124 PET risk adaptation; dose surrogate hit, recurrence signal underpowered.

studies.name: CLERAD-PROBE
studies.tldr: PET-guided risk-adapted adjuvant RIT cut mean blood dose 275 vs 521 mGy (p<0.001) in DTC; recurrence HR 0.38 (0.14-1.05), p=0.06.
details: 🔍 Prospective, randomized, bicentric; N=324 enrolled May 2015 to May 2021 (155 vs 169)
🔍 Adult DTC post-thyroidectomy; unifocal papillary microcarcinoma ≤10 mm excluded

details.text: 💊 Arm 1 (risk-adapted): I-124 PET staging, RIT only if a risk factor present
subdetails: Distant metastases or iodine-avid lesions on PET

details: 💊 Arm 2 (broad): RIT generally performed

details.text: 📊 Outcomes by arm, median f/u 64 mo

details: 📊 I-124 PET upstaged 11 of 78 (14.1%) postoperative T1/T2 N0/Nx pts to N1, prompting RIT
⚠️ EFS is a secondary endpoint with few events; no non-inferiority margin stated in source
⚠️ Sex imbalance: fewer males in Arm 1 (19% vs 34%, p=0.002)
⚠️ Blood dose is a surrogate for secondary malignancy risk, not a measured malignancy outcome
⚠️ Conference abstract only; requires I-124 PET, not widely available

verdict.rationale: Primary endpoint is a dosimetric surrogate; the oncologic safety claim rests on an underpowered secondary EFS endpoint with few events and an arm sex imbalance.
verdict.audience: Adult DTC post-thyroidectomy, excl. unifocal papillary microcarcinoma ≤10 mm

studies.significance: The de-escalation arm was not simple omission: I-124 PET upstaged 11 of 78 (14.1%) T1/T2 N0/Nx pts to N1, adding RIT for occult nodal disease. Selection by functional imaging, not by surgical pathology alone, drives the dose saving (2.5 vs 5.7 GBq), and that gates whether the adjuvant RIT decision transfers to centers without I-124 PET.
studies.monday_clinic: In adult DTC after thyroidectomy with access to I-124 PET, this supports selective rather than routine adjuvant RIT as a dose-sparing strategy; it does not extend to unifocal papillary microcarcinomas ≤10 mm, which were excluded.

primary_endpoint.name: Mean blood dose at complete remission or 18 months

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective, **randomized**, bicentric study; 324 pts enrolled May 2015 to May 2021 (155 Arm 1, 169 Arm 2). Median follow-up 64 months, maximum planned 10 years.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Adult DTC after thyroidectomy, **excluding unifocal papillary microcarcinomas ≤10 mm**. Arms matched for histology, age and tumor stage, but Arm 1 had fewer males (19% vs 34%, p=0.002).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Arm 1 underwent **I-124 PET staging** and received RIT only for incomplete resection, tumor >4 cm, extrathyroidal extent, LN metastases with age ≥45 years, distant metastases, or iodine-avid PET lesions. Arm 2 received RIT generally; administered activity **2.5 vs 5.7 GBq** (p<0.001).

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** mean blood dose at complete remission or 18 months, as a surrogate for secondary malignancy risk. **Secondary:** event-free survival.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Primary endpoint met; oncologic outcomes trended toward Arm 1 (**5 vs 14** progressive/recurrent cases) without reaching p<0.05 for recurrence.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: ESTIMABL2 and IoN addressed RAI omission in low-risk DTC by clinicopathologic selection. CLERAD-PROBE instead uses functional I-124 PET to select, and enrolled a broader population than low-risk only.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents adult post-thyroidectomy DTC staged with I-124 PET at experienced centers. Does not represent unifocal papillary microcarcinoma ≤10 mm or settings without I-124 PET.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Sex imbalance favoring fewer males in the de-escalation arm could bias recurrence toward Arm 1. Bicentric, abstract-only reporting; event-free survival definition and blinding not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The dosimetric gain is unambiguous; the oncologic data argue against harm rather than prove equivalence. Whether lower blood dose translates into fewer second malignancies is untested here.

studies.interpretation:
The cleanest result in CLERAD-PROBE is the one it was built to deliver: a risk-adapted strategy gave less activity and less blood dose, 2.5 vs 5.7 GBq and 275 vs 521 mGy. That outcome was close to guaranteed by design, because one arm withheld treatment from a subset. The question a reader actually brings to the trial is the other one: does withholding adjuvant radioiodine from PET-negative, risk-factor-negative patients cost anything oncologically? On that question the trial is suggestive rather than conclusive. Recurrence ran 5 vs 14 cases with an HR of 0.38 whose interval (0.14-1.05) crosses one, and 5-year EFS was 96.6% vs 91.5% at log-rank p=0.05. The direction is reassuring, and the point estimate even favors de-escalation, but the interval is wide enough to admit both meaningful benefit and no effect, and no non-inferiority margin is described in the source.

The point estimate favoring the de-escalation arm deserves skepticism rather than celebration. A selective strategy outperforming routine treatment on recurrence has no obvious mechanism unless the selection step itself carries therapeutic value or the arms differ at baseline. Both explanations are available. I-124 PET upstaged 11 of 78 patients with postoperative T1/T2 N0/Nx disease to N1, so the risk-adapted arm treated occult nodal disease that conventional staging would have missed, while the broad arm treated without that map. And the arms were imbalanced on sex, 19% vs 34% male, a covariate associated with worse DTC outcomes; an adjusted analysis is not reported in the abstract.

Against ESTIMABL2 and IoN, which tested omission of ablation in low-risk disease selected by clinicopathologic features, CLERAD-PROBE asks a different question. It enrolled all adult DTC except unifocal microcarcinoma ≤10 mm, and it substitutes functional imaging for pathology as the gatekeeper. That makes the trial more ambitious and less generalizable at once: the strategy depends on I-124 PET, which most centers cannot offer, and a reader cannot assume the same safety signal holds if selection reverts to pathology alone, since the PET-driven upstaging is part of what the arm did.

The primary endpoint also needs to be read for what it is. Blood dose stands in for secondary malignancy risk, which is a plausible but indirect link, and the trial does not measure second cancers. For a radiation reader the instinct to minimize unnecessary dose is familiar, yet the clinical payoff here is inferred, not observed, and the absolute late-effect benefit at these activity levels remains unquantified by this study.

What would make the result wrong? A larger trial in which the recurrence HR settles above one, or an adjusted analysis in which the sex imbalance absorbs the EFS separation. What would make it practice-relevant? Confirmation with more events and a prespecified non-inferiority design, or evidence that the PET-guided selection can be approximated without I-124. Until then, CLERAD-PROBE is best read as randomized evidence that selective adjuvant RIT guided by I-124 PET reduces radiation exposure without a detectable oncologic penalty in a modest-event trial, not as proof of equivalence.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: I-124 PET upstaged 11 of 78 (14.1%) T1/T2 N0/Nx pts to N1, so the selective arm treated occult nodal disease while cutting activity 2.5 vs 5.7 GBq. The adjuvant RIT decision moves toward imaging-gated selection, but only where I-124 PET is available.

open_questions: Is PET-guided RIT de-escalation non-inferior for recurrence with more events?
Does lower blood dose translate into fewer second malignancies?
Does the strategy transfer to centers without I-124 PET?

sites.intro: SCRT + PD-1 + consolidation CAPOX vs LCCRT in LARC; EFS is a key secondary and the 1° EP pCR is unreported.

studies.name: UNION
studies.tldr: 3-yr EFS 91.3% vs 77.4%, HR 0.33 (0.15-0.71), for SCRT then camrelizumab + CAPOX vs long-course CRT then CAPOX in LARC.
details: 🔍 Phase 3, randomised 1:1, N=231 (113 vs 118), enrolled July 2021 to March 2023

subdetails: Tumor ≤10 cm from the anal verge
MMR status of enrolled pts not stated; background describes LARC as predominantly pMMR/MSS
Experimental: SCRT 25 Gy/5f → 2 neoadjuvant + 6 adjuvant CAPOX + camrelizumab 200 mg d1, up to 17 cycles
Control: 50.4 Gy/28f + capecitabine 825 mg/m2 BID → 2 neoadjuvant + 6 adjuvant CAPOX
Surgery type and timing not stated in source

details: 📊 BIRC-assessed EFS consistently favored experimental arm; no BIRC numbers in source
⚠️ 1° EP was BIRC-assessed pCR rate; pCR result not reported in this abstract
⚠️ EFS is a key secondary (prespecified α allocation); OS not reported
⚠️ Two variables changed at once: RT schedule (SCRT vs LCCRT) and camrelizumab. RT contribution cannot be isolated
⚠️ Control arm got concurrent capecitabine with RT; experimental arm got no concurrent chemo during SCRT
⚠️ AE denominators (115/112) differ from randomised arms (113/118); as-treated crossover not explained
🔗 SCRT → consolidation chemo backbone echoes RAPIDO and STELLAR; UNION adds PD-1 on top

verdict.rationale: Randomised phase 3 with α-controlled EFS hit, but design confounds RT schedule with PD-1; primary pCR unreported; authors' 'new SOC' claim exceeds a 231-pt, OS-immature dataset.
verdict.audience: cT3-4 or N+ rectal adenocarcinoma ≤10 cm from anal verge

studies.significance: The RT schedule moved alongside the drug: the winning arm used 25 Gy/5f without concurrent chemo against 50.4 Gy/28f with capecitabine, so the EFS gain belongs to the package, not to camrelizumab or SCRT alone. It supports SCRT as the RT platform for IO-containing TNT, without telling you what PD-1 adds to SCRT.
studies.monday_clinic: In cT3-4 or N+ rectal adenocarcinoma ≤10 cm from the verge, this supports SCRT-based TNT with PD-1 as a candidate alternative to long-course CRT; it does not inform dMMR/MSI-H disease or a non-operative strategy, neither addressed in source.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Phase 3, randomised **1:1**, **N=231** (113 experimental, 118 SOC), accrual July 2021 to March 2023. Data cutoff October 1, 2025; median f/u 36.8 vs 35.6 mo.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **cT3-4 or N+** rectal adenocarcinoma, tumor **≤10 cm from the anal verge**. MMR/MSI distribution of enrolled pts not given in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Experimental: **SCRT 25 Gy/5f** with no concurrent chemo. SOC: **50.4 Gy/28f** with concurrent capecitabine 825 mg/m2 twice daily. Target volumes and RT-to-surgery interval not stated.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Both arms: **2 neoadjuvant + 6 adjuvant CAPOX** after RT. Experimental arm adds **camrelizumab 200 mg d1** from CAPOX start, up to 17 cycles.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** BIRC-assessed pCR rate (result not in this abstract). Key secondaries with prespecified α allocation: investigator-assessed EFS and OS.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 3-yr EFS **HR 0.33 (0.15-0.71), P=0.0029**; BIRC-assessed EFS consistent. OS not reported.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G≥3 TRAEs over the whole treatment period **51.3% vs 48.2%**, a small difference despite added PD-1. Irae breakdown and RT-attributable late GI toxicity not reported.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RAPIDO and STELLAR established SCRT followed by consolidation chemo as a TNT platform against long-course CRT. UNION is the first phase 3 to add PD-1 to that platform, but it does not test SCRT-TNT with vs without PD-1.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents operable cT3-4 or N+ LARC within 10 cm of the verge treated with SCRT then CAPOX. Does not represent dMMR/MSI-H disease, upper rectal tumors, or a watch-and-wait pathway.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **Primary pCR endpoint unreported** here, so the EFS headline is a secondary read. AE denominators differ from randomised arm sizes, and with **231 pts** the EFS CI is wide (0.15-0.71).

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The result supports SCRT plus PD-1 plus CAPOX as a package over long-course CRT plus CAPOX. It does **not settle** whether the benefit comes from camrelizumab, from the SCRT-based sequence, or both, nor whether it holds for OS.

studies.interpretation:
The cleanest way to read UNION is as a test of two complete treatment packages, not of a drug. The experimental arm changed the radiation schedule, removed concurrent chemotherapy from the radiation phase, and added a PD-1 inhibitor running through neoadjuvant and adjuvant CAPOX. The control arm kept long-course chemoradiation with capecitabine. An EFS hazard ratio of 0.33 therefore credits the whole experimental sequence, and the abstract's framing of 'an immunotherapy-based regimen' assigns credit the design cannot isolate. For a radiation oncologist the practical question is narrower: does choosing 25 Gy/5f as the RT platform cost anything when systemic therapy is intensified around it? On this evidence it does not, which is useful in its own right.

Against the trials that currently define total neoadjuvant therapy, UNION sits closest to RAPIDO and STELLAR, both of which moved short-course RT plus consolidation chemotherapy into practice as an alternative to long-course chemoradiation. Neither tested checkpoint blockade. UNION extends that SCRT-then-chemo backbone with camrelizumab, and the missing arm is the obvious one: SCRT followed by CAPOX without PD-1. Without it, part of the EFS separation could plausibly reflect the SCRT-based sequence rather than immunotherapy, though the prior trials suggest the backbone swap alone would not be expected to produce a gap this size. That is an inference, not something UNION demonstrates.

Several design features should temper confidence. The primary endpoint was BIRC-assessed pCR, and this abstract reports none of it; the EFS read is a key secondary, protected by prespecified alpha allocation, which is better than an exploratory secondary but still not the question the trial was powered around. With 231 patients, the confidence interval on the HR runs from 0.15 to 0.71, consistent with anything from a large to a modest effect. The 3-year control-arm EFS of 77.4% will be the number readers check against their own long-course CRT outcomes, and the abstract gives no MMR breakdown, so the share of pMMR/MSS disease, the population where PD-1 activity in rectal cancer is genuinely in question, is unknown. The safety denominators (115 and 112) do not match the randomised arms (113 and 118), implying some patients were treated off-assignment; how EFS handled them matters.

On toxicity, G≥3 TRAEs of 51.3% vs 48.2% suggest adding camrelizumab to SCRT-CAPOX did not stack meaningfully on acute toxicity, but the abstract gives no immune-related or late GI/sexual function data, and late radiation effects after SCRT followed by long consolidation are where an RT reader would want follow-up.

What would make the result wrong? A pCR result that fails to separate, an OS curve that converges, or a subgroup showing the benefit concentrated in dMMR tumors would each shift the reading toward a backbone or selection effect. Generalisability outside a single-country PD-1 (camrelizumab) setting also needs confirmation with agents available elsewhere. Until the full paper reports pCR, OS and MMR status, UNION reads as strong support for SCRT as the radiation platform in IO-containing TNT, and as a reasonable but not yet isolated signal for PD-1 in pMMR LARC.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: 25 Gy/5f without concurrent chemo replaced 50.4 Gy/28f with capecitabine and the package won on EFS, so SCRT holds as the RT platform when PD-1 is added. RT's own contribution is not separable, and late toxicity after SCRT plus long consolidation is unreported.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Camrelizumab 200 mg added across neoadjuvant and adjuvant CAPOX, up to 17 cycles, with G≥3 TRAEs 51.3% vs 48.2%. PD-1 benefit in pMMR disease is unproven here because the enrolled MMR mix is not reported and no SCRT-CAPOX-alone arm exists.

open_questions: PD-1 contribution without an SCRT-CAPOX-alone arm
Does benefit hold in confirmed pMMR/MSS tumors?
pCR primary endpoint and OS results

sites.intro: Randomized evidence for SBRT adding local control to modern chemo in non-metastatic pancreas, small N with OS/PFS as secondaries.

studies.name: AGITG MASTERPLAN
studies.tldr: 12-mo locoregional recurrence 20.2% vs 52.0% (P=0.022) with SBRT 40 Gy/5 fx added to chemo; mOS 22.0 vs 14.0 mo (P=0.006).
details: 🔍 Randomized 2:1, chemo + SBRT vs chemo alone; 75 enrolled, 74 eligible, 14 centers

details.text: 🔍 Population: high-risk operable, borderline resectable, or locally advanced pancreatic cancer
subdetails: POPC (n=48): borderline resectable, or operable with ≥1 high-risk feature (>4 cm, extrapancreatic extension, LN+)
IPC (n=26): locally advanced or medically inoperable

details: 💊 3 mo mFOLFIRINOX or gem/nab-paclitaxel (clinician choice), then surgical reassessment
💊 Resected pts: 3 mo adjuvant chemo; unresected pts: 3 more mo systemic chemo
🔍 SBRT 40 Gy/5 fx with fiducial guidance and real-time RT QA

details.text: 📊 Outcomes, chemo + SBRT vs chemo alone
📊 Surgical outcomes, POPC only (31 SBRT vs 17 chemo alone)

details: ⚠️ Only 39 of 49 (80%) assigned to the experimental arm started SBRT
⚠️ No HRs or CIs in source, only medians and P values
⚠️ IPC subgroup n=26; LRR difference there not significant
⚠️ OS and PFS are secondary endpoints in a 74-pt trial

verdict.rationale: Randomized, and the local-control primary was met, but N=74 across mixed resectability groups. The OS gain is secondary, and only 80% of the SBRT arm started RT.
verdict.audience: High-risk operable, borderline resectable or locally advanced pancreatic cancer

studies.significance: The local-control benefit comes from the potentially operable group (12-mo LRR 19.7% vs 52.9%, P=0.031). Inoperable pts had a similar point estimate, but with n=26 it was not significant (P=0.16). The R0 rate was 62% vs 40%, which was not significant. That benefit came from 40 Gy/5 fx with fiducials and real-time QA, delivered between 3 months of induction chemo and surgical reassessment.
studies.monday_clinic: In borderline resectable or high-risk operable pancreatic cancer completing induction mFOLFIRINOX or gem/nab-paclitaxel, this supports SBRT consolidation for locoregional control. For locally advanced or medically inoperable disease it leaves the question open, because the LRR difference there was not significant.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized 2:1**, chemo + SBRT vs chemo alone. 75 pts enrolled at 14 centers, 74 eligible for analysis. Phase not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **High-risk operable, borderline resectable, or locally advanced pancreatic cancer.** 48 potentially operable (POPC: borderline resectable, or operable with a tumor >4 cm, extrapancreatic extension or LN involvement) and 26 inoperable (IPC: locally advanced or medically inoperable).

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **3 months of mFOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel**, chosen by the clinician, then surgical reassessment. Resected pts received 3 more months of adjuvant chemo, and unresected pts 3 more months of systemic chemo.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **SBRT 40 Gy in 5 fractions** with fiducial marker guidance and real-time RT quality assurance. 39 of 49 pts (80%) in the experimental arm started SBRT.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** locoregional recurrence at 12 months. Secondary: PFS, OS, surgical outcomes and toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G3+ toxicity was 70.2% vs 64.0% (P=0.27), **no significant increase** with SBRT. Source gives no breakdown of RT-attributable acute or late GI toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: LAP07 found no benefit from conventional chemoRT after induction gemcitabine in locally advanced disease. Alliance A021501 closed its SBRT arm in borderline resectable disease. MASTERPLAN is a **positive randomized local-control signal** for ablative-intent SBRT on a modern multiagent backbone, a different question from either of those trials.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents borderline resectable or high-risk operable pancreatic cancer after modern induction chemo. Does not represent locally advanced or medically inoperable disease, where the LRR difference was not significant at n=26.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Source reports medians and P values with **no HRs or CIs**, so the size of the OS effect cannot be judged. Source does not say how locoregional recurrence was defined or assessed in unresected pts, which matters for an LRR primary.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The primary endpoint is local control, and it was met. The PFS and OS gains point the same way but are secondary and fragile at this sample size. What remains open is which resectability group carries the benefit and whether the OS signal holds.

studies.interpretation:
The value of MASTERPLAN is that it reopens a question that much of the field had treated as settled against radiotherapy. LAP07 found nothing to gain from conventional chemoradiation after induction gemcitabine in locally advanced disease. Alliance A021501 then closed its SBRT arm in borderline resectable disease. Together these left many medical oncologists treating local therapy in pancreatic cancer as optional. MASTERPLAN differs from both on the things that plausibly matter. It uses an ablative-intent SBRT dose of 40 Gy in 5 fractions with fiducial guidance and real-time QA, after a modern multiagent induction, and its primary endpoint measures what radiotherapy is actually supposed to do. A 12-month locoregional recurrence of 20.2% vs 52.0% is a large separation on the endpoint closest to the intervention's mechanism.

The secondary survival results deserve more caution than the trade-press framing gives them. A median OS of 22.0 vs 14.0 months (P=0.006) in 74 pts, with no hazard ratio or interval reported in the source, is exactly the kind of number that tends to shrink in a confirmatory trial. Small trials that hit a P value overestimate effect size almost by construction. The control arm's 14.0 months is also modest for a population that is two-thirds potentially operable, which raises the question of whether chance imbalance or the small, heterogeneous control arm (randomized 2:1) is flattering the comparison. A local-control gain of this size could plausibly translate into survival in a disease where local progression drives morbidity and some deaths. But a survival claim needs its own powered trial.

Two features cut in opposite directions. Only 39 of 49 pts in the experimental arm started SBRT, so an intention-to-treat analysis dilutes the radiotherapy effect, and the per-treated benefit on local control could be larger than reported. On the other side, the source does not say how locoregional recurrence was ascertained, or how it was defined in a tumor left in place. That is hard to assess on imaging after SBRT, where fibrosis and residual tumor look alike. If assessors knew the allocation, an LRR endpoint is more exposed to bias than OS.

The subgroup split matters for the practical read. The benefit reached significance in the 48 potentially operable pts (19.7% vs 52.9%, P=0.031). The 26 inoperable pts had a similar point estimate (21.4% vs 50.0%) but did not reach significance (P=0.16), which is a power problem, not evidence of no effect. Resection (68% vs 59%) and R0 (62% vs 40%) both moved toward SBRT without reaching significance. The reassuring part is that SBRT did not visibly compromise surgery. The trial cannot say whether it improves margins.

The decision this informs is consolidation SBRT after induction chemo in borderline resectable and high-risk operable disease. MASTERPLAN makes that a defensible option to discuss at tumor board and a strong case for a larger trial. It does not establish a survival benefit, and it does not yet settle locally advanced disease. The result would be wrong if the OS gap reflects a small, unlucky control arm and if LRR ascertainment favored the treated group. A larger trial with a blinded local-failure review is the test.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The local-control benefit comes from the potentially operable group (12-mo LRR 19.7% vs 52.9%, P=0.031). Inoperable pts had a similar point estimate, but the difference was not significant at n=26. The technique was 40 Gy/5 fx with fiducial guidance and real-time QA after 3 months of induction chemo, which supports SBRT consolidation within that sequence.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: SBRT was added to a 3-month induction of mFOLFIRINOX or gem/nab-paclitaxel. mPFS was 11.9 vs 6.3 mo and mOS 22.0 vs 14.0 mo, both secondary endpoints. G3+ toxicity was 70.2% vs 64.0% (P=0.27), so the backbone stayed deliverable with RT added.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: In potentially operable pts, resection was 68% vs 59% (P=0.54) and R0 (>1 mm) 62% vs 40% (P=0.44). Both favor SBRT numerically, but neither is significant at 31 vs 17 pts. So the local-control gain did not come at the cost of resectability, and the trial was too small to show a margin benefit.

open_questions: Does the OS signal hold in a larger randomized trial?
Benefit of SBRT in locally advanced or medically inoperable disease
Does SBRT improve R0 resection rates after induction chemo?

related_trials.brief_title: Locally Advanced Pancreatic Cancer Treated With ABLAtivE Stereotactic MRI-guided Adaptive Radiation Therapy

studies.name: TOP-1 (BOOG 2016-01)
studies.tldr: 5-yr LR 14.8% (95%CI 12.3-17.5) after BCS with no RT and no ET in women ≥70 with low-risk ER+ BC; exceeded the prespecified 10% threshold.

verdict.rationale: Single-arm observational cohort with no RT or ET comparator; benchmark is a registry figure. Large N, but the single-arm gate caps the verdict despite a clear miss of its threshold.
verdict.audience: Women ≥70, ER+ HER2- low-grade T1 BC after BCS, no ET

studies.significance: The trial was powered to exclude a 10% 5-yr LR, and the whole CI (12.3-17.5) sits above it. When neither RT nor ET is given, the counseling figure for this low-risk T1 group is 14.8%, not the single digits implied by ET-backed omission trials. Salvage often reintroduced RT (70 of 123 LR).
studies.monday_clinic: In a woman ≥70 with ER+ ≥50%, HER2-negative, low-grade T1 BC after BCS who will not take ET, this questions RT omission as a low-risk option; it does not bear on RT omission when adjuvant ET is given.

primary_endpoint.name: 5-year local recurrence (invasive ipsilateral)
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: 95%CI 12.3-17.5; above the 10% threshold the trial aimed to exclude

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective, multicenter, observational, **single-arm** cohort. Accrual January 2017 to September 2021, **N=792**, median follow-up **5.1 years** (IQR 4.9-5.2). Cumulative incidence analysis with death as a competing event.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Women **aged ≥70** (median 73.6) with **ER+ ≥50%, HER2-negative** BC, **≤1cm grade 1/2 or ≤2cm grade 1**, and free surgical margins. Under Dutch guidance, ET is not advised in T1 low-grade disease, so **neither RT nor ET was given**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Adjuvant RT was **omitted** after BCS. The 1.3% (99%CI 0.6-2.5%) 5-yr LR risk with RT comes from a national registry, not a concurrent arm.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** 5-yr LR risk, defined as a histologically confirmed invasive ipsilateral event. Secondary: contralateral BC, OS and BC-specific survival. With 800 pts (80% power), the trial was sized to **exclude a 10% 5-yr LR risk**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **5-yr LR 14.8% (95%CI 12.3-17.5)** in 123 pts. Contralateral BC in 32 (4.0%). Of 81 deaths (10.2%), 2 were BC-related.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Salvage of LR was surgical in 114 (92.7%), with **repeat BCS in 86 (75.4%)**. 70 (56.7%) received RT and 43 (35.0%) ET at recurrence.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Earlier RT-omission trials in older women with ER+ disease, such as PRIME II and CALGB 9343, mostly included pts on adjuvant ET. TOP-1 is the population those trials did not test: **ET also omitted**. The LR it found is far above the design's 7.5% expectation.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents women ≥70 with ER+ ≥50%, HER2-negative, low-grade T1 BC after BCS with free margins who receive neither RT nor ET. Does not represent pts taking adjuvant ET, higher-grade or larger tumors, or younger women.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The primary endpoint counts **invasive events only**, so ipsilateral DCIS is outside the 14.8%. The registry benchmark comes from a different population with different case ascertainment, so the RT-attributable gap is approximate. BCSS was reported only descriptively at 5 years.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: On its own prespecified terms, the trial did not show that omitting both RT and ET keeps LR below a level advocates accept. BC-specific mortality was low and salvage was mostly breast-conserving. The authors keep RT omission as a **shared-decision option** for a subgroup, not a default.

studies.interpretation:
TOP-1 answers a question the prior RT-omission literature left open: what local risk remains when both adjuvant RT and adjuvant ET are withheld. Trials such as PRIME II and CALGB 9343 built the case for omitting RT in older women with ER+ disease, but endocrine therapy was part of the treatment in those cohorts and carried some of the local-control load. Dutch guidance, which does not advise ET for low-grade T1 tumors, created a group of women who receive neither treatment. TOP-1 measured that group prospectively, and the result, 14.8% at 5 years, is far from what the investigators expected.

The design benchmark is the key to reading the result. The investigators started from a national registry figure of 1.3% with RT, tripled its upper confidence limit to 7.5% as the expected risk without RT, and sized the study at 800 pts to exclude a 10% risk, a ceiling agreed with patient advocates. The observed 95% CI of 12.3-17.5 lies entirely above that ceiling. So by the trial's own prespecified standard, omitting both treatments in this low-risk group does not keep invasive local recurrence below a level advocates found acceptable. The benchmark was set generously, the cohort is large, and median follow-up reached 5.1 years, so this is a clear negative rather than an underpowered one.

The design limits push confidence in specific directions. With no concurrent RT or ET arm, the RT-attributable increment can only be estimated against a registry figure. That figure comes from a different population, and a registry may undercount recurrences that a protocol with scheduled follow-up would catch. That would narrow the apparent gap, but it cannot move 14.8% below 10%. The primary endpoint also counts only histologically confirmed invasive ipsilateral events, so the total ipsilateral event burden, including DCIS, may be higher than the headline. Using cumulative incidence with death as a competing event is the right method in a cohort where 10.2% died.

What TOP-1 does not settle is whether the excess recurrence costs anything beyond treatment burden. Only 2 of 81 deaths were BC-related, and 114 of the 123 recurrences were treated surgically, 86 with repeat BCS. The cost of omission therefore shows up mainly as salvage: 70 pts received RT and 43 received ET at recurrence, so many ended up having the treatments they had been spared, later and after a second operation. Whether that trade is acceptable depends on the patient's preferences, which is why the authors frame omission as a shared decision. The study also cannot say whether ET alone, without RT, would close most of the gap. That is the open question for an RT reader whose patient declines one treatment but might accept the other.

In practice, the counseling figure changes. For a woman ≥70 with a small, low-grade ER+ tumor who will receive neither RT nor ET, the 5-year invasive LR risk to quote is now 14.8%, not a single-digit figure borrowed from ET-backed omission trials. For women who take ET, the earlier omission evidence still stands, and TOP-1 does not address them.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Omitting RT in women ≥70 with low-grade ER+ T1 tumors who receive no ET gave 5-yr invasive LR of 14.8%, with the full CI above the 10% threshold the trial aimed to exclude. Salvage brought back RT in 70 of 123 recurrences, so omission often delays RT rather than avoiding it.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: With ET also omitted, LR reached 14.8% at 5 years, so the low local risk reported in earlier RT-omission trials relied partly on ET. When RT is being omitted, the decision to skip ET in low-grade T1 disease now carries a measured local cost. ET was given in 43 of 123 recurrences.

papers.title: Omission of adjuvant radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery in systemically untreated older patients with early-stage estrogen receptor positive breast cancer: 5-year results of the TOP-1 study (BOOG 2016-01)
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 545RO · Rapid oral: Breast cancer, early stage · 2026-10-23 · presented by Lotte Bouwman (Leiden, Netherlands)

Background: Adjuvant radiotherapy (RT) following breast-conserving surgery (BCS) is standard of care in women with early-stage estrogen-receptor positive (ER+) breast cancer (BC). Previous studies on RT omission involved older patients treated with BCS and endocrine therapy (ET), showing low local recurrence (LR) risks. According to Dutch guidelines, ET is not advised in T1, low-grade early-stage BC. This study assessed 5-year LR risk after BCS without RT, in older patients with ER+ BC without ET.
Methods: The prospective, multicenter, observational, single-arm TOP-1 study included women aged ≥70 years with low-risk BC (ER+ ≥50%, HER2-negative, ≤1cm and grade 1/2, or ≤2cm grade 1 with free surgical margins). Primary endpoint was 5-year LR risk, defined as a histologically confirmed invasive ipsilateral event. Secondary endpoints included contralateral BC, overall and BC specific survival. Cumulative incidence analysis was performed with death as competing event. With a 1.3% (99%CI 0.6-2.5%; national registry) 5-year LR risk with RT, and the upper CI limit tripled without RT (7.5%), 800 patients (power 80%) were needed to exclude a 10% 5-year LR risk, acceptable to patient advocates.
Results: Between January 2017 and September 2021, 792 patients were included. Median age was 73.6 years (IQI 71.9-75.5). Median follow-up was 5.1 years (IQR 4.9-5.2). In total, 123 patients developed a LR, resulting in a 5-year LR risk of 14.8% (95%CI 12.3-17.5). Treatment of LR was surgical in 114 (92.7%) patients, of whom 86 (75.4%) BCS, 70 (56.7%) patients received RT and 43 (35.0%) ET. Contralateral BC was diagnosed in 32 (4.0%) patients. Death occurred in 81 (10.2%) patients, of whom 2 (2.5%) BC related.
Conclusions: Omission of adjuvant RT resulted in a 5-year LR risk of 14.8% after BCS without ET, in women aged ≥70 with low-grade T1, ER+ BC. Although the LR risk exceeded prior estimates, BCS was possible in most patients and BC specific survival was excellent. Therefore, in a shared decision setting, RT omission is an option for a subgroup of older patients. Follow-up is needed to assess longer-term survival and other secondary endpoints.
Clinical trial identification: National Trial Register: 6147 (however, nowadays outdated). Also registered in the CCMO Research Portal as NL-008797.

papers.title: I-124 PET-guided risk-adapted versus broad adjuvant radioiodine therapy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma: Results from the randomized CLERAD-PROBE trial
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 4210RO · Rapid oral: NETs and endocrine tumours · 2026-10-23 · presented by Kerstin Michalski (Wuerzburg, Germany) · NCT01704586

Background: The role of adjuvant radioiodine therapy (RIT) in differentiated thyroid carcinoma (DTC) remains controversial due to diverging international guidelines. The CLERAD-PROBE trial compares a risk-adapted with a broad RIT strategy regarding blood dose — as surrogate for secondary malignancy risk — and oncological outcomes.
Methods: CLERAD-PROBE is a prospective, randomized, bicentric study (NCT01704586) in adult DTC patients, excluding unifocal papillary microcarcinomas ≤10 mm. Following thyroidectomy, patients in Arm 1 underwent I-124 PET for staging; RIT was administered only if risk factors were present (incomplete resection, tumor >4 cm, extrathyroidal extent, lymph node metastases with age ≥45 years, distant metastases, or iodine-avid lesions on PET). In Arm 2, RIT was generally performed. The primary endpoint was mean blood dose at complete remission or 18 months; the secondary endpoint was event-free survival with a maximum follow-up of 10 years.
Results: 324 patients were enrolled from May 2015 to May 2021 (155 Arm 1, 169 Arm 2). Arms were well-matched for histology, age, and tumor stage; however, Arm 1 included fewer male patients (19% vs. 34%, p=0.002). Notably, I-124 PET upstaged 11 of 78 patients (14.1%) with postoperative T1/T2 and N0/Nx to N1, prompting RIT in these cases. Mean blood dose (275 vs. 521 mGy; p<0.001) and administered activity (2.5 vs. 5.7 GBq; p<0.001) were significantly lower in Arm 1. Median follow-up was 64 months. In Arm 1, risk of progressive or recurrent disease was lower (5 cases in Arm 1 vs. 14 in Arm 2; hazard ratio: 0.38; 95% CI: 0.14-1.05; p=0.06) and event-free survival higher (Log-rank test: p=0.05). Five-year event-free survival was 96.6% in Arm 1 vs. 91.5% in Arm 2.
Conclusions: CLERAD-PROBE demonstrates that a risk-adapted, PET-guided RIT strategy significantly reduces radiation exposure without evidence of inferior oncological outcomes. While the low number of events warrants cautious interpretation, the results support the oncological safety of RIT de-escalation and provide a rationale for a risk-adapted approach in appropriately selected DTC patients.
Clinical trial identification: NCT01704586.

papers.title: Neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy followed by camrelizumab and chemotherapy in locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC): The phase 3 UNION trial
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 3530O · Proffered paper: Gastrointestinal tumours, lower digestive · 2026-10-25 · presented by Zhen Yu Lin (Wuhan, China) · NCT04928807

Background: Despite the use of neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, recurrence and distant metastasis remain common in LARC. Effective immunotherapy-based strategies for the predominantly proficient mismatch repair/microsatellite-stable population remain limited. UNION is the first phase 3 trial to evaluate a neoadjuvant strategy incorporating radiotherapy, immunotherapy, and chemotherapy in LARC. Here we present the prespecified event-free survival (EFS) analysis.
Methods: Patients with cT3-4 or N+ rectal adenocarcinoma (tumor located ≤10 cm from the anal verge) were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive short-course radiotherapy (SCRT; 25 Gy/5f; experimental group) or long-course chemoradiotherapy (50.4 Gy/28f with concurrent capecitabine 825 mg/m2 twice daily; standard of care group) followed by 2 neoadjuvant cycles and 6 adjuvant cycles of capecitabine and oxaliplatin (CAPOX). The experimental group additionally received neoadjuvant and adjuvant camrelizumab (200 mg, day 1) since CAPOX treatment for up to 17 cycles. The primary endpoint was blinded independent review committee (BIRC)-assessed pathological complete response rate. Key secondary endpoints with prespecified α allocation were investigator-assessed EFS and overall survival.
Results: Between July 2021 and March 2023, 231 patients were randomized to the experimental group (n=113) and standard of care group (n=118). As of October 1, 2025, the median follow-up duration was 36.8 months (95% CI, 34.8-37.8) and 35.6 months (95% CI, 34.3-36.9), respectively. The 3-year EFS rate was significantly higher in the experimental group compared with standard of care (91.3% [95% CI, 83.9-95.4] vs 77.4% [95% CI, 67.9-84.4], hazard ratio=0.33 [95% CI, 0.15-0.71], P=0.0029). BIRC-assessed EFS consistently favored the experimental group. During the whole treatment period, the incidence of grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events was 51.3% (59/115) and 48.2% (54/112), respectively.
Conclusions: UNION is the first phase 3 trial to demonstrate a significant improvement in EFS with an immunotherapy-based regimen in LARC. This neoadjuvant strategy represents a new standard of care.
Clinical trial identification: NCT04928807.
